prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B045 as my preferred single achievement, with the same trio and a slightly tighter citation. The scientific core is unchanged: Kane and Mele showed that time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling define a Z2 invariant of the bulk band structure, and that invariant forces protected edge states regardless of microscopic detail. That is a universal mechanism, stated cleanly and analysed rigorously, and it was tested directly when Molenkamp's group measured edge conductance in HgTe wells in 2007. More than fifteen years of independent transport and ARPES work on several material families has not overturned the interpretation. After reading round 1 I have narrowed my claim: the unit I support is the 2D quantum spin Hall effect together with the Z2 concept, not the whole field of topological insulators. That keeps the credit with the people whose work is documented as the origin, and it lets the committee acknowledge the 3D work in background material without reopening the 3D priority question inside a three-name limit.
statement.case_against: The case against is credit and overlap, and round 1 has made it sharper rather than weaker. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the specific HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, Zhang is deceased, and the 3D theorists (Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy) and Hasan are outside any three-name configuration. The 2016 prize on topological phases also means the committee has to argue that Z2 band topology in real materials is a distinct discovery from topological defects and phase transitions; I find that argument defensible but not self-evident, and two other members flag the same overlap. Against this, B022 has the broadest support, a clean two-name attribution and no objection to its science in any file. I therefore treat B045 as conditional: if documentary checking cannot establish that Kane-Mele and the HgTe observation form a self-contained unit that the BHZ proposal does not displace, I would prefer to see B022 awarded cleanly instead of a contested topological citation.

responses.point: She proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, arguing that the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio credits theory twice and omits the first 3D ARPES observation.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously, since a prize that pairs theory with the first observation in each dimension is a coherent principle. But it makes the credit problem larger. Hasan's 3D result rests on theory by Fu, Kane, Moore and Balents, so including him invites the question of why Fu and Moore are absent, while dropping Mele removes half of the author pair who introduced the Z2 invariant in the first place. In a three-name limit I would rather keep one unit that is clean (2D theory and its experimental test) than split the Z2 credit to make room for a different experiment. I would only change if the committee decides the unit is topological insulators in general; then I would want Fu and Moore to be examined openly and would not accept the trio as a quiet compromise.

responses.point: He accepts the same trio, names B022 as his first alternative, and says he would sooner see B022 awarded cleanly than force a contested trio.
responses.response: We are close, and I share your fallback. Our answer to the chair's conditional question should be the same: B022 becomes my choice if documentary checking leaves the BHZ and 3D credit unresolved. I would add one point to your graphene remark. Because the Kane-Mele phase is not realised in graphene, the Z2 classification and the HgTe observation are the real unit, and that supports a citation that names the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, not graphene. On the 2016 overlap I would now put the argument more precisely: that prize recognised topological order in model systems, whereas this one recognises a bulk invariant that classifies real band structures and was verified in a specific material.

responses.point: He holds that the lattice clock has the cleanest credit on the list, that independent laboratories reproduce 1e-18, and that the citation can reward the lattice concept and not clocks in general.
responses.response: I concede more than I did in round 1. Your evidence on independent clock comparisons across RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE is the sort of verification I value, and nobody has argued against the science. My remaining difference is about what counts as the discovery: magic-wavelength trapping and Lamb-Dicke confinement are applications of known atomic physics, so the novelty is the demonstration that many atoms can be held without a first-order light shift. I now accept that this was not obviously possible, and Lindroth and Olsson make that point well. That moves B022 from a reluctant alternative to a prize I could support without reservation about the science; my reservation is only about the 2005 and 2012 overlap, which a lattice-specific citation can address.

responses.point: He ranks baryon acoustic oscillations first as a clue from nature, while conceding the first place reflects his own weighting and that the three-name trio is partly artificial.
responses.response: I share your test of asking whether something is learned about nature and not only about an instrument, and I apply it to the clock as well. But the credit problem you describe is the decisive one for me. The acoustic-peak physics goes back to Peebles and Yu and to Sunyaev and Zeldovich, the detections in 2005 were two large collaborations, and Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock stand for a result in which many people took part. Your point that the committee has given three cosmology prizes since 2006 adds to this. I have not moved B002 into my configuration and would not rank it above B045 or B022 unless there is documentary evidence that the three names stand for the discovery in a way the collaborations do not.

uncertainties: Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize leaves enough room for a distinct prize on Z2 topological insulators; this is the point on which my preference is most likely to change.

Whether documentary checking can settle that Kane-Mele and the HgTe observation form a self-contained unit without the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and without the 3D experiments and theory (Hasan, Fu, Moore, Balents).
Whether Mele or Hasan belongs in a three-name configuration; I favour Mele, but the 3D credit question is only avoided, not solved, by this choice.
B004 and B045 appear to me to be the same discovery; I am relying on memory for the credit history and have not checked it.

If the committee insists on a clean attribution above field-level influence, B022 is the safer prize, and I would not oppose it; I cannot judge the early strontium lattice priority (Katori, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde) from the files.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited candidate: I have no collaboration with, and no institutional tie to, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted names. I work at the University of Gothenburg, in the same physics environment as colleagues Johansson and Olsson at Chalmers, and I note the conflicts that Johansson (B039, B032) and Kroll (B022) have disclosed. I see no reason for either of them to be excluded from discussion of B045, and nothing in the round-1 exchange changes my own disclosure.
